lessons.title: Balance and pan by subtracting, before adding anything
lessons.explanation: All audio in FL Studio passes through the mixer unless it is routed elsewhere, and the mixer page states that the playlist is not bound to any instrument or mixer track, which is why moving a clip can fail to move its mixing destination. Balance has a procedure. The levels page describes it: set the relative instrument levels with the mixer track faders or channel volume knobs, then use the master track fader for the final level, keeping the master from exceeding zero decibels because that is where clipping occurs in the deliverable. The same page gives the rounded decibel values worth remembering, and they are the reason small moves matter: plus six decibels is twice the original level, minus six decibels is half, minus twelve decibels leaves about twenty-five per cent, and plus or minus one decibel is close to the just-noticeable difference. Panning has its own arithmetic: the default circular panning law reduces a centred signal by about three decibels so that its apparent loudness matches hard panning, so a centred instrument is already three decibels down and panning it changes level as well as position. The case for subtracting rather than adding is a combination of headroom and masking. Boosting a part consumes headroom and can make a collision worse, while cutting a narrow band, thinning a voicing or removing a layer leaves room for everything else and keeps the master below the clipping point.
lessons.example: Take guitar, pad and bass with the master peaking slightly above zero decibels, showing the orange peak the manual uses to indicate clipping, and with the pad audible only when the guitar is silent. Name the priority first: the guitar figure carries the material, so it stays. Now change things in order, all of them subtractive. First level: reduce the pad's track fader by six decibels, which is half its previous level, and re-check the master, which should now sit below zero. Second density: reduce the pad from a three-note voicing to one sustained note, which removes two simultaneous contributors without touching any fader. Third, only if the guitar's attacks are still covered, use a narrow equaliser cut on the pad around the guitar's upper band rather than boosting the guitar; the parametric equaliser page describes centre frequency and width as the controls that make a cut narrow. Fourth, panning: a small pan on the pad can help a stereo listener, remembering that the circular panning law had already placed the centred signal about three decibels down and that the separation disappears in mono, so check the mono sum before keeping the pan. Finally, if the master still peaks above zero decibels across the whole mix, prefer a level reduction on the loudest contributor to a limiter applied at the end, because limiting hides a balance problem rather than solving it.
lessons.question: The master peak exceeds zero decibels only where the pad and the guitar sound together, and the proposed fix is a six decibel boost on the guitar plus a limiter on the master. What is the better first response?
lessons.answer: Subtract instead: reduce the pad's level and thin its voicing so the combined signal stays below zero decibels
lessons.distractor: Boost and limit, because a six decibel boost doubles the guitar and a limiter prevents any overshoot
lessons.correction: A boost raises the total signal and pushes the master further toward clipping, and a limiter on the master conceals the balance problem instead of resolving it. Reducing the pad's level by six decibels halves its contribution, and thinning the voicing removes simultaneous contributors, so both the masking and the overload are addressed at their source.

depth.definitions: Balance is the set of relative levels between parts. Headroom is the margin between a signal's level and the ceiling where information is lost, here zero decibels on the master. Clipping occurs when a waveform exceeds the maximum level that can be reproduced, and the manual distinguishes internal floating-point processing, where peaks above zero decibels are not automatically destructive, from the fixed bit-depth output, where they are. A peak meter reports short-lived maxima rather than perceived loudness. The circular panning law is the default rule that reduces a centred signal by about three decibels. Masking is one sound reducing the audibility of another in the same frequency region. A parametric equaliser changes the level of specific frequency bands, with controls for centre frequency and width. Prerequisites are the masking work from lesson 39 and the layer roles from lesson 45.
depth.mechanism: Why is subtracting usually the stronger move? Two mechanisms operate together. The first is arithmetic: levels combine, so two parts at the same nominal level do not stay at that level when they sound together, and any boost applied to a part in a crowded section increases the total that the output must accommodate. The second is perceptual: masking is caused by overlapping energy in the same frequency region, so removing energy from the overlapping part restores the audibility of the masked one without raising anything. A narrow cut is preferable to a wide one because it removes less of the instrument's character, which is a real cost of equalisation and should be stated rather than hidden. Three limits belong here. First, this does not make equalisation or limiting illegitimate; both are tools for specific jobs, and the manual itself suggests a limiter on the master to prevent clipping in a final mix. Second, a balance tuned only in the fullest section will fail in the sparse one, so check the loudest passage and at least one quiet one. Third, internal floating-point headroom does not mean plugin processing is immune to overload, so the practical rule is to keep levels conservative and inspect the output rather than to rely on theoretical margin.
depth.secondExample: Contrast a balance problem in the low register, where the choices are different. If the bass and the pad's lowest note both occupy the region around the bass register, thinning and panning will not help, because low frequencies are difficult to place in the stereo field and the pad's low notes will usually be heard as extra bass rather than as a separate part. The subtractive response here is allocation: let one part own the low note and move the other up a fifth or an octave, which halves or further reduces the frequency of the doubled pitch, and reduce the pad to a single note. A second contrast concerns the order of operations in a session. If a part is out of time or badly tuned, no balance or panning change will make it sound intentional, and the subtractive instinct should be applied to the arrangement instead: remove the part rather than repair it in the mix. The distinction is worth keeping explicit, because a mix can only clarify material that is already playable and in tune.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first equates louder with better, so every comparison is unfair and every processing decision is made at a different listening level; match the approximate level before judging. The second adds a limiter on the master to stop a light from turning orange, which hides an unbalanced mix and leaves the underlying collision intact. The third pans parts hard apart, hears an improvement in stereo and never checks the mono sum, where the separation collapses. The fourth raises the record or monitor level to solve an audibility problem that is actually a routing problem, so the meter changes but nothing reaches the right destination; verify the route by soloing the part and watching which track's meter responds. A fifth error is presentational: describing a mix as balanced when only the quiet section was checked, since the fullest passage is the one that tests the balance.
depth.application: For a fifteen-minute nonblocking task, name the priority in your mix in one sentence, then make at most two subtractive changes and no boosts, keeping a saved copy of the previous state so each change can be undone. Check the loudest four bars and one quiet passage, and listen once in mono. The rubric asks for a stated priority, only subtractive changes, a master that stays below zero decibels in the fullest section, a documented mono check, and monitoring kept at a comfortable level. A model report reads: the guitar carries the figure; the pad lost six decibels, which is half its level, and two of its three notes; the master peaks just below zero in the fullest bar and the collision survives the mono check intact; no equalisation or limiting was needed. If a change does not improve the result, restoring the earlier version is a correct outcome, and saying so is part of the task.
depth.summary: Balance is an argument about priority, and the arithmetic of decibels decides how large a change actually is. You can now solve a crowded mix by removing what is in the way rather than by pushing something above it, and you know why a centred part is already several decibels down. The final lesson takes a piece that is balanced and moving and asks the question that ends more projects than any technical fault: how to decide that it is finished, deliver it, and stop starting new ones.

lessons.title: Finish the piece: render it, listen to the file, and write the delivery note
lessons.explanation: Exporting is not saving. Saving stores the editable project so you can keep working; rendering computes an audio file from the instruments, clips, routing, effects and export options, and the manual points out that saving the project is unnecessary before you can export. Three details decide whether the file contains what you think it does. First, by default the master mixer track is rendered, unless the split mixer tracks option is used, which means any track not routed directly or indirectly to the master will be absent from the render. Second, the length of the render is set by a hierarchy that ends with the tail setting, so a file can legitimately be longer than the counted bars, and the manual's own wording puts the end of the last bar containing data and the tail setting in the same list. Third, sounds from external hardware driven by MIDI are not included unless their audio is recorded and placed as an audio clip, so a hardware part can be perfectly sequenced and completely silent in the file. The manual also states plainly that MIDI is not an audio format, which is the same distinction MIDI.org makes: a MIDI file holds instructions and requires a sound source. Finishing is therefore a procedure rather than a feeling: fix the scope, render, listen to the actual file from the first attack to the end of the tail, log what you heard against what you intended, and then stop.
lessons.example: Apply the procedure to the thirty-two-bar piece from lesson 47 at 100 beats per minute, where the musical body is 32 times 2.4 seconds, which is 76.8 seconds. Render the audio and find that the file is 80.3 seconds long. Subtract to find the difference: 80.3 minus 76.8 is 3.5 seconds. Listen to those final 3.5 seconds with the screen hidden and decide whether they contain an intentional release, such as a reverb tail or a released instrument, or unintended silence. Record the answer, because a 3.5-second unintentional silence is a revision item and a 3.5-second intended tail is a feature. Now check the content rather than the duration: confirm that section A is sparse, that section B gains the filler and melody, that section C drops the beat, and that section D returns. If a part that was driven from the MIDI keyboard through an external keyboard or synth is missing, the cause is the capture type, not the arrangement: the notes were instructions and the sound was never recorded, so either record the audio and place it as a clip or document the dependency. Finally, write the delivery note in four parts, intent, files, listening findings, and next revision, and then declare the piece finished if those four parts agree with one another.
lessons.question: A rendered file is 3.5 seconds longer than the piece's counted body. What has to be established before the file is delivered?
lessons.answer: Whether the extra duration is an intended release, such as a reverb or instrument tail, or unintended silence, by listening against the section plan
lessons.distractor: That the export is invalid, because a render must end exactly at the last bar containing notes
lessons.correction: The manual's render-length hierarchy includes the tail setting, so a file extending past the last bar is expected rather than broken. Note instructions and audible releases are different things, which is why the section plan and a listen decide whether the extra duration was intended. Unintended trailing silence is a revision item, not a mathematical error.

depth.definitions: Rendering computes an audio file from the project's instruments, clips, routing, effects and selected options. A tail is sound continuing after the last scheduled event. Split mixer tracks is an export option that renders individual tracks rather than the master mix. Song mode and pattern mode determine which material the render length is measured from. A MIDI file stores note data and is explicitly not an audio format. A delivery note records intent, files, listening findings and next revision. A stem is a grouped audio contribution, which is not always a single instrument, so do not promise stems when only a full mix was rendered. Prerequisites are the export and delivery work from lesson 40 and the section plan from lesson 47.
depth.mechanism: Why does finishing need a procedure when the music is already written? Because the last step is the only one with a defined end, and every earlier step is open-ended. Leaving a piece unfinished is the default outcome of unlimited refinement, whereas rendering fixes a version, listening supplies the evidence about it, and the delivery note converts that evidence into at most one revision priority. The mechanism behind missed content is worth understanding rather than memorising. A render is a computation over routed material, so anything outside the routed chain, outside the selected range, or outside the set of captured data types is simply not part of the computation: a track routed away from the master, a part that exists only as unrecorded hardware sound, or a range that stops before the intended ending. That is why the checks belong to content, length and listening rather than to a single glance at the file. Two limits must be stated plainly. First, a completed render is evidence about the file, not about musicianship, and a technically valid export can be musically poor. Second, nothing in this lesson was executed here: no project was opened and no file was rendered, so the durations are computed values and the checks are procedures to perform, not observations that were made.
depth.secondExample: Contrast two kinds of unfinished project and the different responses they need. The first is unfinished because of a technical gap: the arrangement is complete and the render is missing a part, which calls for the content checks above and produces a fixed file. The second is unfinished because of an artistic gap: every section exists but nothing ever feels like a final section, which calls for a revision to the material and cannot be repaired by any export setting. A third case is a project that is in fact finished and is being kept open by preference, which is common and worth naming honestly; the way out is to set a bounded stopping rule before the session, such as finishing this piece completely before starting another, and then to hold it. The useful transferable habit is that the stopping rule is decided in advance, when you are not attached to the current version, rather than at the moment when stopping would mean accepting something imperfect.
depth.mistake: Four errors recur. The first declares the work complete because the render finished, without listening to the file end to end; the manual's own point that exporting is not saving is the counterpart of the point that rendering is not listening. The second delivers a project file and expects the recipient to hear what you heard, when a project depends on instruments, plugins and routing that may not travel. The third confuses loudness with completion and describes a file as mastered because it is loud, which conflates a level decision with a finished judgement. The fourth claims a verification that did not happen, such as reporting listening checks on a file that was never opened; a truthful note about an unchecked file is more useful than a confident claim, and the level quiz in this course is not a substitute for a file-level listen.
depth.application: For a twenty-minute nonblocking task, fix the scope of one piece in writing, render it as audio, open the file, and listen from the first attack to the end of the tail at a comfortable level without looking at the project. Record the calculated body length and the actual file length and subtract to get the difference. Then write a delivery note with four headings: intent, files, listening findings, next revision. The rubric asks for a fixed scope stated before rendering, a rendered file that was actually opened and heard, computed durations and their difference, at most one revision priority, and an honest statement of what was not checked. A model note reads: intended a four-section, thirty-two-bar piece at 100 beats per minute, so 76.8 seconds of body; the file is 80.3 seconds, and the extra 3.5 seconds is an intended release; section C's beat drop is audible; the melody is partly covered in section B, so the next revision thins the pad rather than raising the melody; I did not check the file on a second playback device.
depth.summary: A piece is finished when a version is fixed, heard and documented, not when it stops being improvable. Across this level you counted functions rather than labelling chords, derived keys from the circle of fifths, explained borrowed chords by counting the notes they alter, moved harmony with the bass, separated guitar and keys into distinct roles, shaped a melody as a phrase and tested it without the instrument, planned a form whose boundaries are audible, stored movement as automation, balanced by subtraction, and delivered a rendered file with a delivery note. Each of those is a decision you can now state and defend. What none of it does is prove that anything was played, recorded or heard: the arithmetic in this level is computed, the documents were read, and no project was run, so the written and recorded artifacts you produce remain the evidence that matters.

questions.prompt: The first four bars and the second four bars of a melody share their rhythm and their first three pitches, and the second phrase ends on the tonic over the tonic chord. Which structure is this, and what does the ending do?
questions.answer: An aa prime pair, and the tonic ending closes the phrase
questions.distractor: A four-part srdc section in which the tonic ending marks the departure stage
questions.correction: A repeated phrase with a changed ending is labelled a prime rather than a plain repetition, so the pair is aa prime, a two-part structure. Departure is the third stage of an srdc four-part pattern, and closure is produced by the stable final pitch rather than by the repetition of the rhythm.

questions.prompt: A boundary is planned at bar seventeen, but nothing changes audibly there when the piece is played. Which change is most likely to make the boundary register?
questions.answer: Remove a layer at bar seventeen, since a change in instrumentation is one of the surface features that makes a boundary apparent
questions.distractor: Give the section a new name and a different clip colour so the boundary is documented in the arrangement
questions.correction: Names and colours are not on the source's list of features that make a boundary apparent, which includes poetic structure, a rhythmic, harmonic and melodic arrival, a change in instrumentation or volume, and a return to previously heard material. Subtracting a layer satisfies the list and is audible on any playback system.

questions.prompt: A producer records a filter sweep by hand into a pattern and then spends an hour editing individual points. What route would the documentation have suggested instead?
questions.answer: Convert the recorded event data into an automation clip and edit the curve as a shape rather than as individual points
questions.distractor: Render the sweep into audio so the movement can be edited afterwards as a waveform
questions.correction: Recorded movements are stored as event data inside the selected pattern, and the manual notes that at 96 pulses per quarter note an unedited pass can hold hundreds of control points per bar. Converting the recording into a clip makes the movement editable as a curve. Rendering produces audio, after which the control change can no longer be adjusted.

questions.prompt: A mix exceeds zero decibels only in the fullest bar, and the learner's response is a limiter on the master plus a six decibel boost on the melody. What is the better first action?
questions.answer: Subtract on the loudest contributor by reducing its level and thinning its voicing, then re-check the fullest bar
questions.distractor: Add the limiter alone, because the master must not exceed zero decibels under any circumstances
questions.correction: A boost raises the total that the output has to accommodate, and a limiter conceals an unbalanced mix rather than resolving it. Six decibels of reduction halves the contributing part, and thinning a voicing removes simultaneous contributors, so both the masking and the overload are addressed at their source.

questions.prompt: Five sketch projects exist and none of them has been delivered. Which procedure follows this level?
questions.answer: Fix the scope of one piece, render it, listen to the file end to end, and write a delivery note with one revision priority
questions.distractor: Start a sixth sketch so that the strongest idea can be chosen before any of them is finished
questions.correction: Rendering fixes a version, listening supplies the evidence about that version, and the delivery note converts the evidence into at most one revision priority. Starting another sketch defers the only step that has a defined end, since every earlier step is open-ended.

questions.prompt: A loop in G major runs E minor, A minor, D, G, with the roots E, A, D and G. A learner labels the passage a descending-fifths sequence and then calls the closing G a half cadence. Which part of that is right, and what is wrong?
questions.answer: The descending-fifths label is right because each root falls a fifth, but the closing G is a tonic arrival rather than a half cadence, which by definition ends on V
questions.distractor: Both labels are right, because a sequence can end on any chord and a half cadence ends wherever the phrase happens to stop
questions.correction: The root motion E to A to D to G descends by fifth at each step, which is what the sequences chapter names a descending fifths pattern. A half cadence ends on the dominant, so a phrase arriving on the tonic is a tonic arrival in the opposite direction, and the chapter's own definition of the half cadence as ending on V rules the second label out.

questions.prompt: In C major a progression runs C, F, F minor, C, and the third chord is written as F minor with F, its root, in the bass. Which description is accurate?
questions.answer: A flat is borrowed from the parallel minor, the chord is in root position because F is in the bass, and it still carries predominant function
questions.distractor: The chord is a first-inversion A flat major triad because A flat is present and the chord is spelled from the parallel mode
questions.correction: F minor is spelled F, A flat, C, so F in the bass places it in root position and the chord's root stays F. Only one scale degree is borrowed, the lowered sixth. An A flat major triad would be A flat, C, E flat, which is a different collection and would also change the chord's function.

questions.prompt: A pad sounding middle C at about 262 hertz covers a guitar figure in the same range. A learner moves the pad up an octave and reduces its level by six decibels. What are the resulting figures, and does the change address the cause?
questions.answer: About 524 hertz, close to the 523 hertz of C5, and about half the previous level; the register change addresses the overlap, which a level change alone would not
questions.distractor: About 524 hertz and about 75 per cent of the previous level; the level reduction is what removes the overlap
questions.correction: Moving up an octave doubles the frequency, so about 262 hertz becomes about 524 hertz, close to the 523 hertz of C5. Six decibels of reduction halves the contribution rather than leaving three quarters, which would correspond to roughly two and a half decibels. Register separation removes the masking; level alone would only move the competition.

questions.prompt: A learner writes an aa prime melody, plays it back through the sequencer, and reports that the second phrase was heard as closed. What can be concluded?
questions.answer: Only that the sequence played back; an aural check requires singing each phrase unaccompanied, with a contour line or solmization used to record what was heard
questions.distractor: The closed ending is confirmed, because hearing the sequencer play the melody is equivalent to an aural check of it
questions.correction: Playing a sequence verifies that the software produced the notes, not that the writer can hear or reproduce the line. The dictation strategies in the source, contour lines, solmization syllables and protonotation, are the methods that commit a prediction and then test it, and the unaccompanied singing removes the instrument's ability to cover a wrong note.

questions.prompt: A piece is planned as three eight-bar sections at 96 beats per minute, and the third section is meant to be a departure. Compute the section duration and state what the boundary into that section requires.
questions.answer: 2.5 seconds per bar, so each section lasts 20 seconds; the boundary needs a perceptible change such as an arrival, a change of instrumentation or volume, or a return to heard material
questions.distractor: 2.5 seconds per bar, so each section lasts 20 seconds; renaming the section markers is enough once the durations are correct
questions.correction: At 96 beats per minute the beat is 0.625 seconds, so a 4/4 bar is 2.5 seconds and eight bars are 20 seconds. Section length is only half the requirement: the source defines boundaries by what makes them apparent, so a marker that is only a label leaves the boundary inaudible.

questions.prompt: A producer automates the monitor volume knob to rise across the chorus and reports that the rendered file is unchanged. Why is that, and what should have been automated?
questions.answer: The monitor volume knob has no effect on rendered levels, so the track fader or plugin parameter that the render actually uses should have been automated
questions.distractor: The automation was never converted from event data, which is why the rendered level did not change
questions.correction: The manual states plainly that the monitor volume knob is designed to adjust monitoring without affecting the mix level, so automating it changes nothing in the file. Unconverted event data would still have played back during the project, so it would have affected the render rather than leaving it unchanged.

questions.prompt: At 96 pulses per quarter note, how many ticks are in a 4/4 bar, and why does the manual advise care with recorded automation?
questions.answer: 384 ticks, and a continuous recorded pass can create a control point at almost every tick, so converting it to a clip and editing the curve is easier than editing the points
questions.distractor: 96 ticks, because one control point is written per quarter note, so dense automation data cannot occur
questions.correction: At 96 pulses per quarter note a quarter note is 96 ticks and a 4/4 bar is four quarters, which is 384 ticks. The manual's warning about control-point density reflects the fact that a recorded movement can define a new point at nearly every step of the timeline, which is why the recommended route is to convert the recording into an automation clip whose shape can be edited.

questions.prompt: A mix sounds well separated in stereo, but in mono the pad covers the guitar. A learner responds by panning the two parts further apart. What is wrong with that, and what does the three decibel figure refer to in this situation?
questions.answer: Panning collapses when the channels are combined, so the register or density has to change; the three decibel figure is the reduction the default circular panning law applies to a centred signal
questions.distractor: Panning is sufficient if it is increased, and the three decibel figure is the boost that a hard-panned signal receives
questions.correction: Stereo separation disappears in the mono sum, which is why arrangement changes rather than placement changes survive every playback system. The circular panning law reduces a centred signal by about three decibels so that its apparent loudness matches hard panning, so centring a part is already a level decision rather than a neutral one.

questions.prompt: A project sounds complete in the studio, but the render is silent where a part played from external hardware controlled by MIDI should be. Which explanation matches the documentation?
questions.answer: MIDI carries instructions rather than audio, and the hardware's sound has to be recorded and placed as an audio clip for an ordinary offline render to include it
questions.distractor: The MIDI export option should have been chosen instead, because a MIDI file contains the recorded sound of external hardware
questions.correction: The export page's Recording External Hardware section describes making both MIDI and audio connections, recording the sound as it is played, and placing that audio in the playlist before rendering. The same page states that MIDI is not an audio format, so choosing a MIDI file would deliver instructions and no sound at all.

questions.prompt: A 32-bar piece at 100 beats per minute renders to a file of 80.3 seconds. Which statement is correct?
questions.answer: The musical body is 76.8 seconds because 32 bars at 2.4 seconds each, so the extra 3.5 seconds must be listened to and classified as an intended tail or unintended silence
questions.distractor: The musical body is 76.8 seconds, so the extra 3.5 seconds prove that the export settings were wrong
questions.correction: The manual's render-length hierarchy includes the tail setting, so a file legitimately extends past the last bar containing data. Reverb and instrument releases are audible tails rather than errors, and the decision between an intended tail and unintended silence comes from listening to the file against the section plan rather than from the arithmetic alone.

questions.prompt: A loop is A minor, F, C, G. One learner calls it vi-IV-I-V in C major, another calls it i-VI-III-VII in A minor. Which framing is defensible, and what does the choice change?
questions.answer: Both readings use the same pitch classes and the same chords; the difference is where home is heard, and in the second reading the loop begins on the tonic and ends on the dominant
questions.distractor: Only the C major reading is defensible, because the loop contains a G major chord and G is the dominant of C
questions.correction: Roman numerals describe function relative to a tonic, so the same four chords can be analysed from either tonic using the same numerals in different cases. Which reading is more useful depends on where the music sounds like home, and the second reading shows a loop that starts at the tonic and ends on the chord that expects a return, which explains why the cycle can repeat. The presence of G does not settle the question, since the reading from A minor treats G as the seventh-degree chord.

questions.prompt: A learner scores full marks on this level's quiz, owns a sequenced sketch, and has never rendered a file or listened to one. What claim is supported by that evidence?
questions.answer: That the reasoning in the level was checked and an unfinished sketch exists; playing, rendering and file-level listening remain unverified
questions.distractor: That the learner has demonstrated finished-piece delivery competence, since the quiz score and the sketch together are sufficient evidence
questions.correction: The quiz tests the reasoning in the level and the sketch is a saved artifact, but neither involves rendering a file or hearing it end to end, which is what this level's final lesson defines as finishing. This course states that a quiz score is not proof of practical competence, so the honest conclusion names what remains unchecked rather than extending the claim.
